newsitem.title: NEW ZEALAND: OPINION - From the Beehive - Ructions in NZ First.
newsitem.headline: OPINION - From the Beehive - Ructions in NZ First.

text.p: WELLINGTON, Sept 17 - It's been a rough week for those peering through the electoral clouds to discern the shape of New Zealand's first post-MMP coalition government.

New Zealand First, claiming to be the only party that can defeat National, was caught up in internal ructions, first over the way its list was composed, leading to the defection of two of its early stalwarts, and secondly over deputy leader Tau Henare's claim that he would not work in coalition with National, "no matter who is in it".

Henare's stance appeared to conflict with the party's official position on coalition partners. On another front, Henare brushed off speculation that party figures might stage a coup against him after October 12.
Some of the former National figures now in NZ First are said to be worried that public perceptions of Henare as a Maori separatist would cost the party support.
Henare conceded that the party needed "like a hole in the head" publicity about internal dissent.

Officially, NZ First's stance has been not to rule out any coalition possibilities, and it has been relying on winning over onetime National supporters, particularly in rural regions, who could not bring themselves to vote for either Labour or the Alliance. That rural constituency may, however, be frightened off by Henare's vigorous espousal of Maori separatism.

NZ First's troubles have given solace to its opponents. Chief government whip Roger Sowry suggested Henare could be the next victim of "ace manipulator and disgraced former MP Michael Laws". Sowry pointed out that Henare ran the NZ First caucus the day it decided to sack Michael Laws as an MP.

Joining Sowry in rejoicing at NZ First's disarray was Labour's Joe Hawke, who is standing against Henare in Tai Tokerau. Maoris thinking of casting their vote for NZ First should reconsider if the party was intending to politically assassinate one of its leading figures, Hawke said.
Meanwhile NZ First Leader Winston Peters has launched his party's campaign, beating the drum of nationalism, and claiming to be the only genuine "people party".
"We are the only party at this election that is prepared to share power with the people of New Zealand.

"Labour's promise to make New Zealand a better place in 1984 really meant a better place for the rich. National's promise to restore prosperity in 1990 really meant to restore prosperity to Fay Richwhite, Brierleys and the other companies in front of the 'Winebox' inquiry...and through all this the people of New Zealand have suffered, powerless to stop the sell-off of New Zealand."

Peters, strong on rhetoric, offered little, however, for the 150,000 he claimed to be rotting on the dole or an economy he insists is racing into recession with the highest real interest rates in the Western world.

Latest polls show that neither a right-of-centre coalition including National, the Christian Coalition and possibly ACT, nor a Labour-New Zealand First coalition could get a majority in the new parliament. For the opposition parties to govern, the Alliance would have to offer its support.
But the larger question is whether Labour could afford, politically, to go into coalition with New Zealand First, whose strategy is being shaped by Michael Laws.

Labour MPs flinch when they are asked whether they could contemplate working alongside Winston Peters in a coalition cabinet, and they go orbital at the prospect that Peters, as deputy prime minister in such a coalition, would have Laws as his chief of staff, sitting in on the deals essential in a coalition arrangement.

Meanwhile Labour's place in the opinion polls prompted political commentator Colin James to predict it could be finished as a major political force if it does not get more than 20 percent of the party vote on October 12.

National, too, appears to be struggling to lift its core support. It held steady at 35 percent and 38 percent in the latest TV1 and TV3 polls, but growth in support for the Christian Coalition and ACT could be eating away on the fringes.
(Note - The opinions expressed in this article represent the views of the author only. They should not be seen as reflecting the views of Reuters)
